title: Ÿnsect: how the world leader in insects ended up in bankruptcy
publisher: ONEI (Observatoire National de l'Elevage d'Insectes) — advocacy/watchdog NGO

findings.claim: Ÿnsect, long touted as global leader in insect protein, was placed in judicial liquidation and closed its factory; it had raised over EUR 600 million in public and private funding since founding in 2011
findings.systemBoundary: cumulative capital raised, not annual — public (BPI) + private

findings.claim: In 2023 Ÿnsect reported turnover of only EUR 656,000 (excl. internal transactions) yet incurred more than EUR 80 million in losses
findings.systemBoundary: reported financial-year figures

findings.claim: Insect meal remains uncompetitive: its cost is on average 2 to 10 times higher than fish or soy meal
findings.systemBoundary: cost per unit protein meal vs conventional; no method given

findings.claim: The insect-protein failures are structural and sector-wide: Agronutris (raised EUR 100m) entered receivership Jan 2025, Enorm Biofactory (Scandinavian leader, EUR 55m raised) and Aspire Food Group Canada (EUR 42m) went bankrupt; Innovafeed posted EUR 5m revenue and EUR 35m losses in 2024
findings.locator: avsnitt 'A case that is not isolated'
findings.systemBoundary: selected named companies, not exhaustive

findings.claim: The promised circular model failed: health regulations prohibit several waste types, so Ÿnsect turned to agricultural by-products (wheat bran) that compete with existing feed uses and are not waste, undermining the environmental argument
findings.locator: avsnitt 'Far from the promised circular economy'
findings.systemBoundary: feedstock sourcing — regulatory + economic constraint

notMeasured: no systematic sector-wide production/volume data; source is narrative journalism, not a dataset
limitations: Advocacy NGO (ONEI) with a critical stance toward insect farming; financial figures are company-reported/press-sourced; internal date inconsistency (states liquidation 'December 1, 2025' but 'last updated June 30, 2025' and receivership 'March 3, 2025')

title: Ekomatsligan 2024 – En Årsrapport om hållbara offentliga måltider i Sverige
publisher: Ekomatcentrum (The Swedish Centre for Organic Food)

findings.claim: Share of organic food in Swedish public sector fell to 34.2% in 2023, down 2.8 percentage points from prior year; part of a declining trend since 2019 when it was 39%
findings.systemBoundary: share of public-sector food procurement that is organic; survey with 93% participant coverage of municipalities/regions

findings.claim: Of SEK 12.5 billion Swedish public sector spent on food in 2023, organic purchases were only SEK 4.3 billion
findings.systemBoundary: public-sector food spend, value basis

findings.claim: 97% of organic dairy products in Swedish public sector are Swedish-origin vs 79% of conventional; 100% of organic eggs are Swedish vs ~80% of conventional (nearly 20% imported)
findings.systemBoundary: origin share within public-sector procurement, organic vs conventional

findings.claim: Preschools reach 48% organic share, primary schools 42%, upper-secondary 35%, elderly care 29%
findings.systemBoundary: organic share of food by institution type

notMeasured: only 5.7% of municipalities measure climate impact per served portion; most measure per kilo purchased, so full meal life-cycle climate footprint is largely unmeasured
limitations: Advocacy organization promoting organic food; self-reported survey of municipalities (93% coverage); framing is explicitly pro-organic

title: Ekologisk animalieproduktion 2024
publisher: Jordbruksverket (Swedish Board of Agriculture) — official statistics JO0609

findings.claim: Swedish organic milk delivered to dairies was 295,200 tonnes in 2024, down 18% vs 2023 and down 39% from the 2021 peak; organic share of total delivered milk fell to just under 11% in 2024 (from ~17% 2018–2021)
findings.systemBoundary: milk delivered/weighed-in at dairies (invägning), not on-farm production; organic = fully converted per EU 2018/848

findings.claim: Slaughter weight of organically reared cattle was 16,200 tonnes in 2024 (−13% vs 2023, −28% vs 2019 peak); organic share of total Swedish cattle slaughter fell to just under 12% (from 16% in 2019)
findings.systemBoundary: slaughter weight of animals reared organically and delivered from converted producers; NOT meat finally sold as organic in shops

findings.claim: Slaughter of organic pigs fell 48% between 2023 and 2024 to 2,400 tonnes (−64% since 2021 peak), lowest since measurement began 2009; organic share of total pig slaughter fell to 1%
findings.locator: seksjon 'Får och lamm, grisar samt slaktkyckling', tabell 3-4
findings.systemBoundary: slaughter weight; organic share of total Swedish pig slaughter

findings.claim: Organic egg wholesale intake was 14,000 tonnes in 2024, −13% vs 2023, organic share 13% of total (lowest since 2010)
findings.systemBoundary: wholesale intake (~85% of total organic egg production per source), organic share

findings.claim: Organic sheep and lamb slaughter was ~600 tonnes in 2024 (−17% vs 2023, −47% vs 2018), organic share 15% of total (down from 23% peak in 2016)
findings.locator: seksjon 'Får och lamm, grisar samt slaktkyckling'
findings.systemBoundary: slaughter weight; organic share of total sheep/lamb slaughter

notMeasured: slaughter statistics do NOT measure how many animals are finally sold as organic or the amount of organically-labelled meat in shops — only available organic raw material; poultry slaughter tonnage relies on expert-estimated average slaughter weight; egg statistics cover only wholesale (~85% of total)
limitations: Official statistics; quality flagged as good for cattle/sheep milk/eggs but pig slaughter sensitive to register-linkage problems and broiler tonnage depends on expert estimate; only ~40% of organic milk intake traceable to reported products

title: Dagligvare: Forskjeller i innkjøpspriser ytterligere redusert

findings.claim: Konkurransetilsynet's 2023 mapping shows Norgesgruppen gets lower purchase prices from suppliers than Coop and Rema, but the gap has narrowed continuously and is substantially reduced since 2017
findings.systemBoundary: purchase-price differences between the three chains for goods both buy, computed on one chain's purchase volume ('netto nettopriser'); actual magnitude withheld as commercially sensitive

findings.claim: The mapping covers 22 suppliers from 16 companies (Tine, Mills, Nortura, Orkla, Ringnes, Coca-Cola, Mondelez, Scandza, Mars, Nestlé, Kavli, Maarud, Dr. Oetker, P&G, Lerum, Swedish Match) from 2020 (16 suppliers/10 companies earlier)
findings.systemBoundary: sample of large branded suppliers, not full supplier universe

notMeasured: actual size of the purchase-price differences is not published (commercially sensitive); part of the narrowing is attributed to Rema/Coop offering more counter-services and campaigns rather than genuine price convergence
limitations: Magnitudes withheld; difference partly reflects counter-services (logistics, merchandising, campaigns) not pure price; agency recommended NOT to introduce price regulation

title: Konkurransetilsynets dagligvarerapport 2024

findings.claim: Norwegians buy roughly 95% of their food from one of the three big chains; the market is a highly concentrated oligopoly with high entry barriers
findings.systemBoundary: share of grocery trade through the three big chains (physical stores)

findings.claim: Total grocery-market turnover grew from NOK 208 billion (2020) to NOK 227 billion (2024), +9.1%, driven by falling unit sales from 2021 and rising prices from 2022
findings.systemBoundary: traditional grocery market, physical store sales only; excludes petrol/service trade and non-food in Normal/Europris

findings.claim: NorgesGruppen is the largest chain nationally with 43.5% of turnover in 2024; market shares have been stable, NorgesGruppen declining most and Rema increasing most over 2020-2024
findings.systemBoundary: national turnover share, physical grocery stores; based on turnover figures reported to NielsenIQ

findings.claim: Coop holds ~48.8% of turnover in the 50 least-populous municipalities vs NorgesGruppen 41.8% in the 5 most-populous; chains have strongly uneven regional presence
findings.systemBoundary: turnover share within named municipality groups

findings.claim: Kiwi has overtaken Rema as the largest low-price chain (Rema was largest until 2023); low-price segment gained 4.8 pp of turnover 2020-2024, mostly at the expense of broad-assortment stores
findings.systemBoundary: segment share of total turnover

findings.claim: On 21 Aug 2024 Konkurransetilsynet fined Coop ~NOK 1.3 bn, NorgesGruppen ~NOK 2.3 bn and Rema ~NOK 1.3 bn for illegal price-information exchange (mutual price-hunting access) that restricted competition Jan 2011–April 2018; parties held >95% combined share; decision appealed Feb 2025
findings.systemBoundary: regulatory decision (under appeal to Konkurranseklagenemnda); covers price-collection cooperation, not proven overcharge amount

findings.claim: Margin study: chains had high margins in 'chocolate and snacks' and 'soft drinks', low margins in 'meat', 'seafood' and 'eggs'; chains' gross margins on own-brand goods were 12 pp lower than on mapped branded goods; returns exceeded what a competitive market would predict
findings.systemBoundary: profitability 2017-2021 and product-level margins 2020–H1 2023; branded sample selected for strong brands, not comparable to own-brand assortment

findings.claim: Tine receives 93% of deliveries from Norwegian dairy farmers and is the clearly largest actor in nearly all major dairy markets; from 1 Nov 2024 the target-price system was replaced by a volume model giving Tine alone control over the raw-milk price, which the authority warns risks larger price increases over time
findings.systemBoundary: share of Norwegian raw-milk deliveries to Tine

findings.claim: Grocery consumer prices rose 11.5% (Dec 2021–Dec 2022), 8.9% (2023) and 4% (2024) per SSB; the national market has ~4,000 individual stores
findings.systemBoundary: SSB consumer price index for groceries, Dec-Dec

notMeasured: actual size of purchase-price differences (withheld); the authority did not conclusively decide whether to regulate purchase prices; competitive harm from the meierimarked volume model is a forward-looking risk assessment, not a measured effect
limitations: Market-share method uses chain-reported turnover to NielsenIQ without adjustment; excludes online/petrol/service trade and non-food; fine decision under appeal

title: Årsrapport for Daglegvaretilsynet 2022

findings.claim: In Daglegvaretilsynet's 2022 cooperation-climate survey (Kantar Public, fieldwork June-Sept 2022), 61-80% of suppliers agreed the cooperation is mainly based on honesty, predictability and loyalty; NorgesGruppen scored clearly better than REMA 1000 and Coop, while Bunnpris and Oda scored better still
findings.systemBoundary: quantitative survey of suppliers rating the five largest chains (n≈54-146 per chain); measures perception, not conduct

findings.claim: Nearly 20% of suppliers reported experiencing a grocery chain imitating the supplier's idea or brand (EMV/copycat); chains in turn believe 18% of leading suppliers do the same
findings.systemBoundary: self-reported survey experience of imitation, both directions

findings.claim: NorgesGruppen is perceived as worst on using delisting as harassment/reprisal; suppliers report price changes should be handled better, especially by Coop; a serious finding was prevalence of missing written agreements and verbal side-agreements
findings.systemBoundary: survey perception ratings

findings.claim: Daglegvaretilsynet operated with only 3.98 FTE in 2022 (target was 5); nearly all cases/inquiries related to the three biggest chain groupings NorgesGruppen, Coop and REMA 1000; the Nordic UTP supervisory bodies (NO/SE/FI/DK) held a joint meeting in May 2022
findings.systemBoundary: agency staffing

notMeasured: the survey identifies WHICH cooperation issues are problematic but explicitly does not explain WHY; cannot separate fear from tough-but-legal competition vs breaches of the Good Trading Practice Act; no formal cases were opened in 2022 (all handled by dialogue)
limitations: Very small agency; findings rest on perception survey and supplier accounts that cannot be verified; agency was uncertain whether a purchase-terms regulation would help consumers

title: Produksjon av økologiske jordbruksvarer: Rapport for 2025 (Rapport nr. 4/2026)

findings.claim: 43.4 million litres of organic milk were delivered to dairies in Norway in 2025 (marginal decline from 2024); 35 million litres were resold as organic milk (the largest volume ever registered), giving an application rate ('anvendelsesgrad') of 80% — there was not enough organic milk to meet demand
findings.systemBoundary: milk delivered to dairies vs share actually sold labelled organic; the remaining 20% is sold as conventional

findings.claim: About 3,135 tonnes of organic meat (cattle, pig, poultry, sheep, lamb) were produced in Norway in 2025, +1.1% from 2024; only 41% of reported organic meat from four-legged animals was actually used/sold as organic (all poultry meat was used as organic)
findings.systemBoundary: produced organic meat vs share sold as organic; 59% of four-legged organic meat sold as conventional

findings.claim: Just over 4,700 tonnes of organic eggs were produced in Norway in 2025 (marginal increase), with an application rate near 88%
findings.systemBoundary: produced vs used as organic

findings.claim: Organic food sales in Norwegian grocery retail reached NOK 4.3 billion in 2025, up 17.6% from 2024 (vs +6.4% for total grocery market); organic share of the grocery market is stable at around 2% (2.3% counting only categories with an organic alternative)
findings.systemBoundary: grocery-retail scan data (NielsenIQ), incl. both Norwegian and imported organic goods; excludes non-grocery channels

findings.claim: Organic share by grocery category in 2025: dairy 3.0%, vegetables 3.7%, eggs 10.6%, baby food 37.7%, meat 0.7%, beverages 1.0%; dairy overtook vegetables as the largest organic category (NOK 836m)
findings.systemBoundary: organic share within each grocery category (NielsenIQ)

findings.claim: Organic grain production estimated ~16,100 tonnes in 2025-2026 (+7%); organic grain area fell 1.7% to 76,515 dekar; Norwegian share of organic milling wheat used by flour mills was 60% in 2025 — Norwegian share of organic feed raw material is stable but substantially lower than for conventional feed
findings.systemBoundary: preliminary delivery data Jul-Jun season; Norwegian-origin share of organic milling wheat

findings.claim: Internationally the organic agricultural area held stable while global organic food sales reached a new record in 2024; Switzerland had the highest organic market share and per-capita consumption, closely followed by Denmark and Austria
findings.systemBoundary: international comparison; implies Norway's ~2% organic share is far below Denmark/Switzerland leaders

contradicts.what: Both NO and SE report declining/stagnant organic livestock shares, but Sweden's organic milk share (~11%) and cattle-slaughter share (~12%) are higher than Norway's ~2% overall organic grocery share; the two use different denominators (SE = share of production; NO = share of retail sales), so figures are not directly comparable

notMeasured: the report tracks only a selection of sales channels, so total organic sales are larger than the sum reported; oversupply relative to demand means an unmeasured share of organic production is sold as conventional (captured only via 'anvendelsesgrad')
limitations: Preliminary delivery data for 2025-2026 season with modelled restleveranser (10-15% assumed delivered Mar-Jun); retail figures from NielsenIQ; report is an input to agricultural negotiations

title: Circular Food Systems: A content and discourse analysis of the Swedish case (KTH MSc thesis)
publisher: KTH Royal Institute of Technology (Erik Bojö, MSc thesis)

findings.claim: The study's own contribution is a qualitative content/discourse analysis of Swedish magazine and media articles over five years (plus interviews with Ragn-Sells, Axfoundation, Foodhill); it identifies four narratives of circular economy in Swedish food (combat food waste, combat plastic packaging, business opportunity, net good for sustainability), with processing companies the most common stakeholder group
findings.systemBoundary: discourse/content analysis of media texts + 3 interviews; maps stated actor intentions, not realised material flows or outcomes

findings.claim: Sweden's three largest grocery chains ICA, Coop and Axfood together control over 90% of the market, making the Swedish grocery market the most concentrated in the EU; Sweden has about 2,800 food-producing companies (third-largest industry by turnover)
findings.systemBoundary: secondary citation from Livsmedelsföretagen (industry org); Bojö is not the primary measurer

findings.claim: In 2021, 0.91 million tonnes of food waste (86 kg per capita) arose in the Swedish food sector; global food-sector GHG emissions are estimated at ~25% of total global emissions
findings.systemBoundary: secondary citation of Naturvårdsverket food-waste statistics; thesis does not measure this itself

notMeasured: the thesis explicitly does not quantify realised material flows, emissions reductions or circularity outcomes — it maps discourse and stated expectations; it notes actors 'expect' circularity to reduce emissions and increase self-sufficiency but does not verify these expectations
limitations: MSc thesis; findings limited to what appears in Swedish media/magazines and 3 interviews; method-limitation section acknowledges selection and interpretation bias; quantitative figures are secondary citations

title: Unlocking bacterial potential to reduce farmland N2O emissions
publisher: Nature (Hiis et al.), NMBU / IIASA / Veas WWTP

findings.claim: Fertilizing soil with biogas-production digestate in which the N2O-respiring bacterium Cloacibacterium sp. CB-01 had grown to ~6×10^9 cells/ml reduced N2O emissions by 50-95% depending on soil type, in field experiments
findings.systemBoundary: field experiments on specific soil types; effect measured on N2O flux from digestate-amended plots, not full life-cycle

findings.claim: Scaling the data to the European level, national anthropogenic N2O emissions could be reduced by 5-20% (more if including other organic wastes)
findings.systemBoundary: model-based scale-up from field data to European national emissions; a potential, not a realised reduction

findings.claim: Farming-induced (direct + indirect) N2O emissions account for >50% of total anthropogenic N2O; global total anthropogenic N2O was 4.1-10.3 Tg N2O-N/yr for 2007-2016; liming acidified soils reduces N2O by 10-20% but with near-neutral net climate effect due to CO2 from lime
findings.systemBoundary: global emission estimate cited from a comprehensive 2007-2016 analysis (ranges reflect uncertainty)

notMeasured: the paper does not measure realised deployment or aggregate N2O reduction at national scale — the 5-20% is a model projection; long-term durability beyond the field-trial window and effects across all soil types are not fully established
limitations: Field trials on selected soils; European scale-up is an extrapolation; authors note the effect is ascribed to the strain's tenacity in soil rather than superior biokinetics

title: Delivering the Circular Economy – A Toolkit for Policymakers: Denmark Case Study (Potential for Denmark as a Circular Economy)
publisher: Ellen MacArthur Foundation (with McKinsey / Danish EPA)

findings.claim: For the Danish food & beverage sector, cascading bio-refineries capturing full value of by-product and waste streams (pork/dairy processing, agricultural residual biomass) could yield a modelled net value of EUR 300-500 million annually by 2035 (EUR 50-80m by 2020)
findings.systemBoundary: scenario estimate to 2035 vs business-as-usual; adoption-rate × addressable value-pool × net-value-per-unit; not a realised or measured flow

findings.claim: Reducing Danish avoidable food waste from 80-90 kg/capita to 40-50 kg/capita (a ~30-50% reduction) could save households and businesses an estimated EUR 150-250 million annually by 2035 (EUR 30-40m by 2020)
findings.systemBoundary: scenario reduction target and associated saving; baseline waste figure is directional; benchmarked to SITRA Finland study

findings.claim: Danish households spent over EUR 23 billion on food and beverages in 2013 (20% of total household consumption); the pork and dairy deep-dive covered 5.4 million tonnes of material streams
findings.systemBoundary: cited national consumption statistic; the 5.4 Mt is the addressable material-stream pool for the modelling, not a measured recovered flow

notMeasured: all sector benefit figures are forward-looking 2020/2035 scenario estimates, explicitly 'directional' and reliant on numerous assumptions; the report states it does not recommend specific policy and that findings cannot be directly transposed to other countries
limitations: Draft/confidential 2015 modelling exercise; economy-wide CGE + opportunity modelling; Denmark-specific and dated; a policymaker toolkit, not measurement of actual circular flows

title: Summary of the Swedish Competition Authority's inquiry into the food industry 2023–2024 (Report 2024:5)

findings.claim: Swedish food inflation reached around 26% between February 2022 and March 2023; the Authority concludes cost increases were passed on to consumers to varying degrees, and grocery retailers largely defended or increased their gross margins in SEK, indicating weak price competition
findings.systemBoundary: food CPI Feb 2022–Mar 2023; margin analysis of the food value chain

findings.claim: The Swedish grocery retail market is dominated by four vertically integrated players with own wholesale operations — Ica, Axfood, Coop and Lidl; a fifth, City Gross, was recently acquired by Axfood; concentration has increased through acquisitions
findings.systemBoundary: national grocery retail; retail competition is local, wholesale national

findings.claim: In one-third of Sweden's 290 municipalities there are only one or two established grocery retailers; there are no discount stores in 102 of 290 municipalities, so about one million residents lack access to a discount store in their municipality (discount presence is linked to lower local food prices)
findings.systemBoundary: count of municipalities and residents without local discount store access

findings.claim: The Swedish food supply chain comprises 160,000 companies with 300,000 employees; the food manufacturing industry had turnover of just over SEK 220 billion (~EUR 20.5 billion) in 2022, with ~56% of net sales and ~61% of value added created in companies with more than 250 employees
findings.systemBoundary: national food supply chain per Statistics Sweden business classification

findings.claim: Primary production concentration has increased over 15 years in arable crops, milk and pig production; two large agricultural cooperatives dominate — Lantmännen (owned by 18,000 Swedish farmers; brands Axa, Kungsörnen, Scan) and Arla Foods amba (Danish-registered, ~8,000 dairy farmers of whom ~2,000 Swedish)
findings.systemBoundary: cooperative ownership counts

findings.claim: Norway (unlike Sweden) can require companies in concentrated sectors such as grocery to notify ALL acquisitions incl. minority stakes and can intervene in local markets; Denmark can also intervene in local geographic mergers (e.g. Salling Group/Aldi required to divest); Sweden's merger control only reaches effects on a substantial part of the country
findings.systemBoundary: comparison of NO/DK/SE merger-control powers

notMeasured: the Authority did NOT examine whether the described agreements/collaborations (e.g. coordinated product-launch/range-revision windows among ICA, Axfood, Coop) are compatible with the Competition Act's prohibition on anti-competitive agreements — it studied the industry as a whole, not individual conduct; profitability analysis and shrinkflation study were ongoing/unfinished
limitations: Summary of multiple underlying reports; methodology in the source reports; no law-enforcement conclusion on named practices; English translation Dec 2024

title: Dagligvaruhandelns etablering i kommunerna (Konkurrensverkets rapport 2024:4)

findings.claim: Sweden's grocery market is highly concentrated: Ica alone has a market share above 50%; the five largest (Axfood, City Gross, Coop, Ica, Lidl) together held nearly 99% of national turnover in 2022
findings.systemBoundary: national turnover market share; source is industry map (DLF/Delfi) plus authority calculations

findings.claim: There were about 3,200 grocery stores in Sweden in 2022: Ica ~1,300, Axfood ~830 (Willys 234 own + Hemköp 202), Coop ~820, Lidl 205 (wholly owned), City Gross 42; Lidl's long-term goal is to grow from 205 to 300 stores
findings.systemBoundary: store counts per DLF/Delfi and company sources

findings.claim: Market concentration has fallen somewhat over 20 years: in 2000 the three largest (Ica, Coop, Axfood) held over 97%; by 2022 the top-three share had dropped to about 88%, mainly due to Netto's and Lidl's low-price entry 2002-2003; Netto exited Sweden in 2019 (Coop bought its 162 stores)
findings.systemBoundary: top-3 national market share over time

findings.claim: More than every third Swedish municipality (102 of 290) lacked a discount store in 2022, meaning ~1 million residents have no discount store in their municipality; in several municipalities only two of the five largest chains are established; the five big chains' store count grew ~2% (2014-2021), with low-price Willys and Lidl growing 16%
findings.systemBoundary: municipality-level count of discount-store presence and residents affected

notMeasured: the report does not resolve whether limited local competition is caused mainly by municipal planning or by chains' own conduct — it documents both and the disagreement between municipalities and chains over cause
the study focuses on establishment barriers, not on measuring price effects directly
limitations: Market-share and store-count figures rest on industry sources (DLF/Delfi Dagligvarukartan) plus authority estimates; different sources give different total store counts; read partially (intro, market-structure and conclusions sections)

title: Hvorfor mislyktes Lidl med å etablere seg på det norske markedet? En kvalitativ casestudie
publisher: Norges Handelshøyskole (NHH), Selmani & Førre, MSc (del av FOOD-prosjektet)

findings.claim: The study concludes Lidl's failure in Norway (established 2004, withdrew 2008, ~50 stores at peak) was driven by the Norwegian import protection ('importvern'/tariffs), a poorly-adapted product assortment, insufficient preparation, a geographically broad roll-out that created distribution problems, and Norwegian consumer reluctance to unfamiliar products; Reitan Gruppen took over Lidl's store locations and staff
findings.systemBoundary: qualitative case study based on semi-structured interviews with Norwegian grocery-industry informants; explanations are informant interpretations

findings.claim: In 1995 four large groupings held 97% of the Norwegian grocery market (growing); this grew to about 99% (citing Sørgard 2003); Lidl had earlier established in Finland (2001) and Sweden (2003)
findings.systemBoundary: secondary citation of market-share figures within the thesis

findings.claim: An informant (Rema, via Tom Kristiansen) reported Lidl believed it could lower the Norwegian grocery price level by 15-20%, which Rema judged unrealistic given their own purchasing conditions; Lidl's country manager reportedly said that even with a 45% gross margin they would not have been profitable because their scale was too small
findings.systemBoundary: informant recollection/opinion; the 15-20% is a claimed intention, not a measured effect

notMeasured: informants disagree on how much room there was for new entrants (one claims the market was saturated with more stores per capita than Sweden in 2004); the thesis is qualitative and does not quantify the price effect of import protection or the counterfactual of Lidl succeeding
limitations: MSc case study on interviews conducted ~15-20 years after the events (recall bias); explanations are informant perspectives, not measured causation; market-share figures are secondary citations

title: NOU 2013: 6 God handelsskikk i dagligvarekjeden
publisher: Norges offentlige utredninger (Norwegian public inquiry / government-appointed committee)

findings.claim: Norwegian supplier markets are highly concentrated: the three largest suppliers (CR3) usually hold over 80% share, a share below 70% is an exception, and the lowest CR3 the Matkjedeutvalget found is over 60%; all but one of the examined product groups has an HHI over 2,000 (indicating high concentration); import-protected markets stand out with especially high concentration
findings.systemBoundary: CR3 supplier market share per product group (2010 data from Matkjedeutvalget); measures upstream supplier concentration, not retail

findings.claim: Low-price stores account for over 50% of turnover in the Norwegian grocery market and are the single most important sales channel; Norway is among the countries where the largest share of food is bought through grocery chains, with very few alternative distribution channels
findings.locator: kap. 5 s. ~25 (siterer NILF, Dagligvarehandel og mat 2013 s. 31)
findings.systemBoundary: low-price segment share of total grocery turnover

findings.claim: Store proximity is the most important reason for choice of store for 3 of 4 consumers (76%), rising to 88% for ages 18-29 and 84% in Oslo/Akershus; grocery ranks below average in BI's customer-satisfaction survey (8,000 customers), with fruit/vegetables and meat the least satisfying markets in 2012
findings.systemBoundary: consumer survey on store-choice drivers and satisfaction

notMeasured: the committee did not have capacity to map home-delivery/online channels (godtlevert.no, retthjem.no); the report notes HHI must be used with caution as it does not reliably indicate profit/competition intensity under price competition
limitations: 2013 committee report; concentration figures are secondary citations from Matkjedeutvalget (2010 data) and are now dated; read partially (summary and concentration chapters)

title: ICA Gruppen Annual Report 2024

findings.claim: ICA Gruppen's consolidated net sales rose 6.5% to SEK 157,216 million in 2024 (from 147,645); operating profit excl. items affecting comparability was SEK 6,884 million (+8.2%)
findings.locator: Board of Directors' report; five-year summary p. 33
findings.systemBoundary: consolidated group net sales (ICA Sweden, Rimi Baltic, Apotek Hjärtat, ICA Bank, ICA Real Estate); audited self-report

findings.claim: ICA Sweden is the leading Swedish grocery retailer with almost 1,300 stores (independent retailers own/operate their stores under agreements with ICA Sweden); Rimi Baltic runs some 315 wholly-owned stores (84 Estonia, 140 Latvia, 91 Lithuania) with a combined regional market share around 13%; Apotek Hjärtat has almost 400 pharmacies and over 32% pharmacy market share
findings.systemBoundary: store counts and market shares self-reported (Rimi share from country statistics, pharmacy from Apoteksföreningen)

findings.claim: Food waste in ICA warehouses and stores was 1.27% by weight in 2024, down 30% relative to the 2016 base year (target: halve by 2025); food is stated to account for approximately one quarter of total human climate impact
findings.systemBoundary: food waste in warehouses+stores (Swedish and Baltic operations) as % by weight of food sold, per FLW Protocol; excludes upstream/consumer waste

findings.claim: Emissions from ICA's own operations fell to 82,441 tonnes CO2e in 2024 (from 97,983 in 2023, 101,399 in 2022), i.e. 0.52 tCO2e per SEK m turnover; climate impact from food sold was reported at 1.87 (unit stated as tonnes CO2e per kg food sold, likely kg CO2e/kg); ICA has SBTi-approved net-zero-by-2050 targets covering Scope 1, 2 and 3, incl. 42% absolute Scope 1&2 cut by 2030
findings.systemBoundary: Scope 1&2 own operations measured; Scope 3 food-sold intensity is company-calculated; the 1.87 unit label appears to be a typo (tonnes vs kg)

notMeasured: the report does not disaggregate realised material/nutrient flows (N-P-K) or supply-chain-level food waste beyond warehouses/stores; private label share of sales is stated to be 'growing' but not given as a precise figure in the sections read
limitations: Self-reported corporate annual report (audited financials; sustainability data on company methodology); climate intensity per kg food is a modelled/calculated metric; read partially (overview, BoD report, sustainability summary)
